10.1177/1745691616635612.results_passage: This meta-analysis of working memory training studies (87 publications, 145 experimental comparisons) found reliable improvements on measures of intermediate transfer (verbal and visuospatial working memory) immediately following training. 10.3389/fnut.2025.1664412.results_passage: Thirteen RCTs involving 612 participants were included. Plasma sitosterol and campesterol concentrations were increased by on average 2.24 μmol/L (31%) and 5.00 μmol/L (37%), respectively, compared to control, while total- and LDL-cholesterol were reduced by on average 0.36 mmol/L (5.9%) and 0.33 mmol/L (8.5%), respectively. The increase in sitosterol and campesterol was impacted by the dose of PS, the baseline PS concentration and the PS composition of the test products, with the highest dose category (2.0-3.2 g/d) showing increases of 3.56 and 7.64 μmol/L. Intake of PS-enriched foods increases plasma sitosterol and campesterol concentrations, although total plant sterols remain below 1% of total sterols circulating in the blood.

10.1016/j.numecd.2025.104433.license: Copyright Elsevier (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1016/j.numecd.2025.104433.results_passage: Nine RCTs (n = 1337 participants) met the inclusion criteria for this systematic review and meta-analysis of Mediterranean diet interventions. Compared with control diets, Mediterranean diet interventions significantly reduced glycated hemoglobin (mean difference -0.18), LDL cholesterol (-0.10), and triglycerides (-0.20), with no significant effects observed on fasting glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, total cholesterol, or HDL cholesterol. A qualitative gut-microbiota analysis showed increased alpha-diversity and enrichment of health-related taxa, including Akkermansia muciniphila and Roseburia spp. Mediterranean diet interventions improve HbA1c, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides, and promote beneficial gut-microbiota changes that may contribute to the metabolic benefits of the diet.

10.1016/j.numecd.2020.12.032.license: Copyright Elsevier (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1016/j.numecd.2020.12.032.results_passage: A total of 37 guidelines, 108 systematic reviews, and 20 RCTs were included in this review of foods and LDL cholesterol. With high evidence, foods high in unsaturated and low in saturated and trans fatty acids, with added plant sterols/stanols, and high in soluble fiber (e.g. oats, barley, and psyllium) caused at least moderate (0.20-0.40 mmol/L) reductions in LDL cholesterol, while unfiltered coffee caused a moderate to large increase. With moderate evidence, avocados and turmeric caused moderate to large reductions, and pulses, hazelnuts, walnuts, high-fiber/wholegrain foods, and green tea caused small to moderate reductions, whereas sugar caused a small increase. Several foods distinctly modify LDL cholesterol levels, and the results may aid future guidelines and dietary advice for hypercholesterolemia.

10.1093/aje/153.4.353.license: Copyright Oxford University Press (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1093/aje/153.4.353.results_passage: Fourteen published trials of coffee consumption were identified and pooled using a random-effects model. A dose-response relation between coffee consumption and both total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol was identified (p < 0.01), with increases in serum lipids greater in studies of patients with hyperlipidemia and in trials of caffeinated or boiled coffee. Trials using filtered coffee demonstrated very little increase in serum cholesterol. Consumption of unfiltered, but not filtered, coffee increases serum levels of total and LDL cholesterol.

10.1210/jc.2009-2430.license: Copyright The Endocrine Society (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1210/jc.2009-2430.results_passage: Nine healthy subjects were studied once after a night of normal sleep duration and once after a night of 4 hours of sleep, using hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp studies to measure insulin sensitivity. Sleep restriction resulted in increased endogenous glucose production during the clamp study compared to the unrestricted night, indicating hepatic insulin resistance, and decreased the glucose disposal rate during the clamp, reflecting decreased peripheral insulin sensitivity. Sleep restriction decreased the rate of glucose infusion by approximately 25% and increased plasma nonesterified fatty acid levels during the clamp study. Partial sleep deprivation during only a single night induces insulin resistance in multiple metabolic pathways in healthy subjects, a finding that may be relevant for variations in glucoregulation in patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

10.1007/s40279-015-0365-0.license: Copyright Springer (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1007/s40279-015-0365-0.results_passage: Twenty-eight studies with 723 participants met the inclusion criteria for this meta-analysis comparing high-intensity interval training (HIT) and endurance training on VO2max. The meta-analysed effect of endurance training on VO2max was a possibly large beneficial effect (4.9 mL/kg/min) compared with no-exercise controls, and there was likely a large beneficial effect of HIT (5.5 mL/kg/min) compared with no-exercise controls. When compared with endurance training, there was a possibly small beneficial effect for HIT (1.2 mL/kg/min), with additional improvements for typically longer HIT repetitions, older subjects, and interventions of longer duration. Endurance training and HIT both elicit large improvements in the VO2max of healthy, young to middle-aged adults, with the gains being greater following HIT when compared with endurance training.

10.1152/japplphysiol.00322.2023.license: Copyright American Physiological Society (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1152/japplphysiol.00322.2023.results_passage: Forty-one adults with stable coronary artery disease were randomized to 8 weeks of Finnish sauna use or a control intervention. After the sauna intervention, resting core temperature was lower and sweat rate during sauna exposure was greater, but the change in brachial artery flow-mediated dilation did not differ between interventions. The change in central arterial stiffness, systolic, and diastolic blood pressure also did not differ between interventions. Four sessions of Finnish sauna bathing per week for 8 weeks does not improve markers of vascular health (endothelial function, microvascular function, arterial stiffness, or blood pressure) in adults with stable coronary artery disease, despite evidence of heat acclimation.

10.1007/s40279-021-01562-2.license: Copyright Springer (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1007/s40279-021-01562-2.results_passage: From 11,981 records, 58 studies were included in this systematic review, with 54 providing data for meta-analysis of resistance training and body composition. Compared to control, resistance training reduced body fat percentage by -1.46%, body fat mass by -0.55 kg, and visceral fat by a standardised mean difference of -0.49. Measurement type was a significant moderator in body fat percentage and body fat mass, but sex was not, and training volume and training components were not associated with effect size. Resistance training reduces body fat percentage, body fat mass and visceral fat in healthy adults.

10.1080/02640414.2020.1754716.license: Copyright Taylor & Francis (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1080/02640414.2020.1754716.results_passage: Of 1669 articles identified, 22 were included in the qualitative analysis and 18 were meta-analysed for this review of exercise and resting metabolic rate (RMR). Exercise interventions (aerobic and resistance exercise combined) did not increase resting metabolic rate (mean difference: 74.6 kCal/day, P = 0.10), and there was no effect of aerobic exercise alone on RMR (mean difference: 81.65 kCal/day, P = 0.25). However, resistance exercise increased RMR compared to controls (mean difference: 96.17 kCal/day, P = 0.0002). This systematic review effectively synthesises the effect of exercise interventions on RMR in comparison to controls, despite heterogenous methodologies and high risk of bias within included studies.

10.3945/ajcn.115.119339.license: Copyright American Society for Nutrition (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.3945/ajcn.115.119339.results_passage: Young men were randomly assigned to a lower-protein (1.2 g/kg/d) or higher-protein (2.4 g/kg/d) diet during a 4-week marked energy deficit combined with intense exercise training. Lean body mass increased in the higher-protein group (1.2 kg) and to a greater extent compared with the lower-protein group (0.1 kg), and the higher-protein group had a greater loss of fat mass (-4.8 kg vs -3.5 kg). All measures of exercise performance improved similarly in both groups with no effect of protein supplementation. Consumption of a diet containing 2.4 g protein/kg/d was more effective than 1.2 g protein/kg/d in promoting increases in lean body mass and losses of fat mass when combined with a high volume of resistance and anaerobic exercise.

10.1016/j.numecd.2024.103805.license: Copyright Elsevier (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1016/j.numecd.2024.103805.results_passage: Twenty RCTs were included in this systematic review and meta-analysis comparing isocaloric intermittent fasting (IF) and caloric restriction (CR). IF groups had significant reductions in fat mass (kg) and interleukin-6 in the short term, and fat mass (%), waist circumference, fasting blood insulin and HOMA-IR in the long term, while CR groups had significantly lower hunger, fatigue, and triglycerides. IF may be an effective alternative to CR but is not superior to CR in enhancing human health. Due to the low number of long-term studies, future studies should focus on longitudinal randomized trials comparing IF and CR in different populations, age groups, and IF patterns.

10.7326/0003-4819-153-7-201010050-00006.license: Copyright American College of Physicians (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.7326/0003-4819-153-7-201010050-00006.results_passage: Ten overweight adults underwent 14 days of moderate caloric restriction with either 8.5 or 5.5 hours of nighttime sleep opportunity in a randomized crossover study. Sleep curtailment decreased the proportion of weight lost as fat by 55% (1.4 vs. 0.6 kg with 8.5 vs. 5.5 hours of sleep) and increased the loss of fat-free body mass by 60% (1.5 vs. 2.4 kg; P = 0.002). This was accompanied by markers of enhanced neuroendocrine adaptation to caloric restriction, increased hunger, and a shift in relative substrate utilization toward oxidation of less fat. The amount of human sleep contributes to the maintenance of fat-free body mass at times of decreased energy intake, and lack of sufficient sleep may compromise the efficacy of typical dietary interventions for weight loss and related metabolic risk reduction.

10.1016/j.archger.2025.106063.license: Copyright Elsevier (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1016/j.archger.2025.106063.results_passage: Twelve randomized trials (n = 459) were included in this meta-analysis of branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) supplements combined with resistance training in sarcopenic older adults. Only skeletal muscle index significantly improved with the combined intervention versus control (SMD = 0.337, p = 0.029). No significant differences were found in hand grip strength, 30-second chair stand, Short Physical Performance Battery, walking speed, knee extension strength, total lean mass, or fat mass. BCAA supplementation post-resistance training only increased skeletal muscle index in older adults, without improving other functional or body composition outcomes.

10.3389/fnut.2026.1893033.license: Copyright Frontiers Media (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.3389/fnut.2026.1893033.results_passage: Seven randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies were included in this meta-analysis of acute caffeine supplementation in military personnel under sleep loss. Compared with placebo, caffeine significantly improved vigilance and response performance under conditions of sleep deprivation or sleep restriction (SMD = 0.73), complex cognitive performance (SMD = 0.54), and military task performance (SMD = 0.45). The ergogenic effects of caffeine were most consistent for vigilance and response performance, showed stable beneficial effects on complex cognitive performance, and were primarily reflected in improved task-execution speed and operational efficiency for military task performance. The available evidence suggests that acute caffeine supplementation improves vigilance and response performance during sleep loss in military personnel, with additional benefits for complex cognitive and military task performance, supporting caffeine as a practical short-term adjunct to fatigue management during military operations.

10.1179/147683010X12611460764840.license: Copyright Taylor & Francis (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1179/147683010X12611460764840.results_passage: The combination of 97 mg L-theanine and 40 mg caffeine was compared to placebo on cognitive performance, alertness, blood pressure, and heart rate in a sample of 44 young adults. The combination of moderate levels of L-theanine and caffeine significantly improved accuracy during task switching and self-reported alertness (both P < 0.01) and reduced self-reported tiredness (P < 0.05). There were no significant effects on other cognitive tasks, such as visual search, choice reaction times, or mental rotation. The results suggest that 97 mg of L-theanine in combination with 40 mg of caffeine helps to focus attention during a demanding cognitive task.

10.1002/hup.2259.license: Copyright John Wiley & Sons (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1002/hup.2259.results_passage: This meta-analysis identified randomised controlled trials with data on memory (K = 13), executive function (K = 7) and attention (K = 8) testing whether Ginkgo biloba enhances cognitive function in healthy individuals. Effect sizes were non-significant and close to zero for memory (d = -0.04), executive function (d = -0.05) and attention (d = -0.08). Meta-regressions showed that effect sizes were not related to participant age, duration of the trial, daily dose, total dose or sample size. Ginkgo biloba had no ascertainable positive effects on a range of targeted cognitive functions in healthy individuals.

10.1111/psyp.12736.license: Copyright Wiley/Society for Psychophysiological Research (not in PMC, no reuse licence found)
10.1111/psyp.12736.results_passage: Based on data from 40 experimental studies, this meta-analysis confirmed a small effect of aerobic exercise on time-dependent measures (g = .35) and accuracy (g = .22) in executive function tasks. Preadolescent children (g = .54) and older adults (g = .67) benefited more from aerobic exercise than other age groups when reaction time was considered as the dependent variable, whereas aerobic fitness and the executive function component had no influence on the obtained effect sizes. High aerobic fitness is no prerequisite for temporary improvements of the executive control system, and low- as well as high-fit individuals seem to benefit from exercise in a similar way. Preadolescent children and older adults in particular might strategically use a single aerobic exercise session to prepare for a situation demanding high executive control.

10.1136/bmj-2023-075847.results_passage: 218 unique studies with a total of 495 arms and 14170 participants were included. Compared with active controls, moderate reductions in depression were found for walking or jogging (Hedges' g -0.62, 95% CI -0.80 to -0.45), yoga (g -0.55, -0.73 to -0.36), strength training (g -0.49, -0.69 to -0.29), mixed aerobic exercises (g -0.43, -0.61 to -0.24), and tai chi or qigong (g -0.42, -0.65 to -0.21). The effects of exercise were proportional to the intensity prescribed. Exercise is an effective treatment for depression, with walking or jogging, yoga, and strength training more effective than other exercises, particularly when intense.

10.1136/bjsports-2025-110301.license: Not in PMC; BMJ CC BY-NC (re-use restricted, non-commercial only per journal notice)

Exercise reduced depression (standardised mean difference (SMD)=-0.61, 95% CI -0.69 to -0.54) and anxiety (SMD=-0.47, 95% CI -0.59 to -0.36) symptoms, with aerobic exercise demonstrating the most substantial impact on both depression and anxiety symptoms. The greatest benefits by population group for depression were seen in emerging adults aged 18-30 and postnatal women. Greater reductions in depression were associated with exercise in group and supervised settings. Exercise of shorter duration and at lower intensity was most strongly associated with anxiety reduction.

Larger effects were found among healthy participants (delta = 0.50, 95% CI 0.22-0.78) compared to participants with a physical or mental illness (delta = 0.19, 95% CI 0.06-0.31). RET significantly improves anxiety symptoms among both healthy participants and participants with a physical or mental illness.

10.3389/fpubh.2023.1259250.results_passage: 11 randomized controlled trials involving 1,824 participants were included. All these studies demonstrated positive effects of mindfulness therapy on depression (SMD = -0.33, 95% CI: [-0.44, -0.22], p < 0.00001), anxiety (SMD = -0.35, 95% CI: [-0.46, -0.25], p < 0.00001), stress (SMD = -0.39, 95% CI: [-0.48, -0.29], p < 0.00001) and sleep quality scores (SMD = -0.81, 95% CI: [-1.54, -0.09], p = 0.03). 10.1016/j.psyneuen.2023.106415.license: Not in PMC (Elsevier, not open access)

A random effects meta-analysis on cortisol as measured in blood, saliva or hair found that stress management interventions outperformed pooled control conditions with a medium positive effect size (g = 0.282). Studies using cortisol awakening measures (g = 0.644) revealed larger effects than those measuring diurnal cortisol (g = 0.255). Mindfulness and meditation (g = 0.345) and relaxation (g = 0.347) interventions were most effective at changing cortisol levels, while mind body therapies (g = 0.129) and talking therapies (g = 0.107) had smaller and non-significant effect sizes.

10.1177/070674371305800702.license: Not in PMC (SAGE/Can J Psychiatry, not open access)
10.1177/070674371305800702.results_passage: 115 studies met inclusion criteria. The mean effect size of 94 comparisons from 75 studies of CBT and control groups was Hedges g = 0.71 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.79), corresponding to a number needed to treat of 2.6. This may be an overestimation as there were strong indications of publication bias (adjusted g = 0.53), and the effect size of higher-quality studies was significantly lower (g = 0.53) than lower-quality studies (g = 0.90). CBT is an effective treatment for adult depression, although the effects may have been overestimated until now.

10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2023.3971.results_passage: Data from 65 RCTs were included with 5048 participants. Third-wave cognitive behavior therapies (SMD, -0.76 [95% CI, -1.15 to -0.36]), CBT (SMD, -0.74 [95% CI, -1.09 to -0.38]), and relaxation therapy (SMD, -0.59 [95% CI, -1.07 to -0.11]) were associated with reduced GAD symptoms vs treatment as usual. When excluding studies at high risk of bias, relaxation therapy lost its superiority. Only CBT remained significantly associated with greater effectiveness than treatment as usual at 3 to 12 months follow-up. CBT may represent the first-line therapy of GAD.

10.1159/000502891.license: Not in PMC (Karger, not open access)
10.1159/000502891.results_passage: 19 studies met inclusion criteria. Bright light therapy (BLT) was superior over placebo with a standardized mean difference of -0.37 (95% CI: -0.63 to -0.12) for depression ratings (18 studies, 610 patients) and a risk ratio of 1.42 (95% CI: 1.08-1.85) for response to active treatment (16 studies, 559 patients). No evidence for publication bias was found, but there was moderate heterogeneity and a moderate-to-high risk of bias. BLT can be regarded as an effective treatment for seasonal affective disorder, but larger high-quality trials are needed.

10.1192/bjpo.bp.115.001610.license: CC BY-NC-ND (No Derivatives -- figure reuse not permitted)
10.1192/bjpo.bp.115.001610.results_passage: A meta-analysis including 881 participants from 20 RCTs demonstrated a beneficial effect of light therapy in non-seasonal depression (standardised mean difference in depression score -0.41, 95% CI -0.64 to -0.18). This estimate was associated with significant heterogeneity (I2=60%, P=0.0003) not sufficiently explained by subgroup analyses, and there was high risk of bias in the included trials. Light therapy may be effective for patients with non-seasonal depression and can be a helpful additional therapeutic intervention, but overall quality of evidence is poor.

10.1038/s41398-019-0515-5.results_passage: 26 studies with 2160 participants were analyzed. The meta-analysis showed an overall beneficial effect of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids on depression symptoms (SMD = -0.28, P = 0.004). Compared with placebo, EPA-pure (100% EPA) and EPA-major formulations (>=60% EPA) demonstrated clinical benefits with an EPA dosage <=1 g/d (SMD = -0.50, P = 0.003, and SMD = -1.03, P = 0.03, respectively), whereas DHA-pure and DHA-major formulations did not exhibit such benefits. Omega-3 PUFAs with EPA >= 60% at a dosage of <=1 g/d would have beneficial effects on depression.

10.1017/S0033291724001697.results_passage: 31 trials with 24189 participants were analyzed. Each 1000 IU/day vitamin D3 supplementation slightly reduced depressive symptoms in individuals with and without depression (SMD: -0.32, 95% CI -0.43 to -0.22). The effect was more pronounced in those with depressive symptoms (SMD: -0.57, 95% CI -0.69 to -0.44). The greatest reduction occurred at 8000 IU/day (SMD: -2.04, 95% CI -3.77 to -0.31). Trials with follow-up <=8 weeks and 8-24 weeks showed stronger effects than those lasting 24-52 weeks or longer than 52 weeks. Vitamin D3 supplementation had no significant effects on anxiety symptoms.

10.1002/14651858.CD000448.pub3.license: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews copyright (not a CC licence; PMC deposit, standard copyright, not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD000448.pub3.results_passage: A total of 29 trials (5489 patients) including 18 comparisons with placebo and 17 comparisons with synthetic standard antidepressants met the inclusion criteria. In nine larger trials the combined response rate ratio (RR) for hypericum extracts compared with placebo was 1.28 (95% CI, 1.10 to 1.49); in nine smaller trials it was 1.87 (95% CI, 1.22 to 2.87). Compared with tri-/tetracyclic antidepressants and SSRIs, RRs were 1.02 (95% CI 0.90-1.15) and 1.00 (95% CI 0.90-1.11) respectively. Hypericum extracts are superior to placebo, similarly effective as standard antidepressants, and have fewer side effects than standard antidepressants.

10.1080/1028415X.2025.2602153.license: Not in PMC (Taylor & Francis, not open access)
10.1080/1028415X.2025.2602153.results_passage: 34 RCTs comprising 1769 participants were included. Saffron supplementation significantly reduced scores on the BDI (14 trials, 817 participants; WMD = -4.39, 95% CI: -6.64 to -2.15, p < 0.001) and the BAI (6 trials, 339 participants; WMD = -5.06, 95% CI: -8.44 to -1.68, p = 0.003). No significant effects were observed for the HDRS, HARS, or POMS. The certainty of evidence was rated as moderate. Saffron supplementation may be an effective complementary intervention for reducing self-reported depressive and anxiety symptoms in adults; lack of clinician-rated effects underscores the need for high-quality trials.

10.1186/s12888-025-07644-z.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (No Derivatives -- figure reuse not permitted)
10.1186/s12888-025-07644-z.results_passage: 72 RCTs were included (3,319 intervention and 2,778 control participants). The meta-analysis demonstrated significant reductions compared to placebo in depression (SMD = -0.53, 95% CI: -0.67 to -0.39, P < 0.001) and anxiety (SMD = -0.44, 95% CI: -0.59 to -0.28, P < 0.001). Probiotics also improved sleep quality (SMD = -0.39, 95% CI: -0.53 to -0.25, P < 0.001). Subgroup analyses indicated that probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics independently alleviated anxiety and depression, with effects varying by population, intervention duration, and probiotic type.

10.1097/MD.0000000000036005.results_passage: 635 records were initially identified, with 4 studies ultimately included. Concerning cognitive outcomes, a statistically significant moderate improvement was found with probiotic supplementation. For depressive symptoms, the overall effect was negligible and not statistically significant. Heterogeneity was low (I2 = 0% for both outcomes) and no significant publication bias was detected, though caution is advised due to the limited number of studies. Probiotics may enhance cognitive domains and mitigate depressive symptoms, emphasizing the gut-brain axis role, but more standardized research is needed.

10.1007/s00127-022-02261-7.results_passage: 32 studies were included; the majority focused on depression. Narrative synthesis found most studies show loneliness at baseline is associated with subsequent new onset of depression; the few studies on anxiety and self-harm also showed a positive association. Meta-analysis of eight independent cohorts found a pooled adjusted odds ratio of 2.33 (95% CI 1.62-3.34) for risk of new onset depression in adults who were often lonely compared with people who were not often lonely, interpreted with caution given evidence of heterogeneity. Loneliness is a public mental health issue associated with the onset of depression and other common mental health problems.

10.1111/add.14935.license: Not in PMC (Wiley, not open access)
10.1111/add.14935.results_passage: 42 studies (338,426 participants) were analyzed. Alcohol use disorders (AUD) were associated with significantly increased risk of subsequent depressive symptoms (relative risk [RR] = 1.57, 95% CI = 1.41-1.76). Heavy drinking had an increased risk of depressive symptoms, but the association was only significant when controls were limited to non-heavy drinkers (RR = 1.13, 95% CI = 1.05-1.22); this became non-significant after adjusting for publication bias and confounders. A J-shaped association was observed where light-moderate drinking had a significantly decreased risk of depression, while heavy drinking showed no significant association compared with non-drinkers.

10.1037/bul0000410.license: Not in PMC (APA journal, not open access)
10.1037/bul0000410.results_passage: 1,338 effect sizes across 154 studies were included (N = 5,717; ages 7-79 years). All forms of sleep loss resulted in reduced positive affect (standardized mean difference [SMD] = -0.27 to -1.14), increased anxiety symptoms (SMD = 0.57-0.63), and blunted arousal in response to emotional stimuli (SMD = -0.20 to -0.53). Findings for negative affect, emotional valence in response to stimuli, and depressive symptoms were mixed and depended on the type of sleep loss. This is the most comprehensive quantitative synthesis of experimental sleep and emotion research to date, showing that extended wakefulness, shortened sleep duration, and nighttime awakenings adversely influence human emotional functioning.

10.1016/j.ssmph.2021.100934.results_passage: 50 studies were included (16 RCTs, 18 controlled studies, 16 uncontrolled before-and-after studies) out of 14,321 records screened. Random effects meta-analysis of RCTs showed that nature-based interventions (NBIs) were effective for improving depressive mood (-0.64, 95% CI: 1.05 to -0.23), reducing anxiety (-0.94, 95% CI: 0.94 to -0.01), improving positive affect (0.95, 95% CI: 0.59 to 1.31), and reducing negative affect (-0.52, 95% CI: 0.77 to -0.26). The most effective interventions were offered for between 8 and 12 weeks, with optimal dose ranging from 20 to 90 minutes. NBIs, specifically gardening, green exercise, and nature-based therapy, are effective for improving mental health outcomes in adults.

10.1056/NEJMsa1211128.license: Not in PMC (NEJM, not open access)
10.1056/NEJMsa1211128.results_passage: Smoking and cessation histories from 113,752 women and 88,496 men were related to causes of death occurring by December 31, 2006. For participants 25 to 79 years of age, the rate of death from any cause among current smokers was about three times that among those who had never smoked (hazard ratio for women, 3.0; hazard ratio for men, 2.8). Life expectancy was shortened by more than 10 years among current smokers. Adults who quit smoking at 25-34, 35-44, or 45-54 years of age gained about 10, 9, and 6 years of life respectively, compared with those who continued to smoke. Cessation before age 40 reduces the risk of death associated with continued smoking by about 90%.

10.1016/S2468-2667(21)00302-9.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (No Derivatives -- figure reuse not permitted)
10.1016/S2468-2667(21)00302-9.results_passage: 15 studies (47,471 adults, 3013 deaths, median follow-up 7.1 years) were included. Compared with the lowest quartile of steps per day, the adjusted hazard ratio (HR) for all-cause mortality was 0.60 (95% CI 0.51-0.71) for quartile 2, 0.55 (0.49-0.62) for quartile 3, and 0.47 (0.39-0.57) for quartile 4. Restricted cubic splines showed progressively decreasing mortality risk among adults aged 60+ with increasing steps per day until 6000-8000 steps/day, and among adults younger than 60 until 8000-10000 steps/day. Taking more steps per day was associated with a progressively lower risk of all-cause mortality, up to a level that varied by age.

10.1093/eurjpc/zwad229.license: Not in PMC (Oxford University Press, not open access)
10.1093/eurjpc/zwad229.results_passage: Seventeen cohort studies with 226,889 participants and median follow-up of 7.1 years were included. A 1000-step increment was associated with a 15% decreased risk of all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.81-0.91), while a 500-step increment was associated with a 7% decrease in cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.93; 95% CI 0.91-0.95). Using a restricted cubic splines model, a nonlinear dose-response association between step count and both all-cause and cardiovascular mortality was observed, with progressively lower mortality risk with increased step count, more the better over a cut-off of about 3867 steps/day for all-cause mortality and 2337 steps for cardiovascular mortality.

10.1001/jama.2009.681.license: Not in PMC (JAMA, not open access)
10.1001/jama.2009.681.results_passage: Data were obtained from 33 eligible studies (all-cause mortality: 102,980 participants, 6910 cases; CHD/CVD: 84,323 participants, 4485 cases). Pooled risk ratios (RRs) of all-cause mortality and CHD/CVD events per 1-MET higher level of maximal aerobic capacity were 0.87 (95% CI 0.84-0.90) and 0.85 (95% CI 0.82-0.88) respectively. Compared with participants with high cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), those with low CRF had an RR for all-cause mortality of 1.70 (95% CI 1.51-1.92) and for CHD/CVD events of 1.56 (95% CI 1.39-1.75). Better CRF was associated with lower risk of all-cause mortality and CHD/CVD.

10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.6185.results_passage: 107 cohort studies (4,838,825 participants, 425,564 deaths) yielding 724 risk estimates were analyzed. Adjusting for potential confounding from sampling variation, former-drinker bias, and other study-level quality criteria, the meta-analysis found no significantly reduced risk of all-cause mortality among occasional (>0 to <1.3 g ethanol/day; RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.86-1.06) or low-volume drinkers (1.3-24.0 g/day; RR 0.93, P=.07) compared with lifetime nondrinkers. Risk increased significantly for drinkers consuming 45-64 g/day (RR 1.19) and 65+ g/day (RR 1.35), with larger risks among female drinkers than male drinkers. Daily low or moderate alcohol intake was not significantly associated with all-cause mortality risk, while increased risk was evident at higher consumption levels, starting at lower levels for women than men.

10.15288/jsad.2016.77.185.license: Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs -- standard PMC copyright notice, no Creative Commons licence found (not reusable)
10.15288/jsad.2016.77.185.results_passage: A systematic review and meta-regression analysis of 87 studies (3,998,626 individuals, 367,103 deaths) investigated alcohol use and mortality risk. Without adjustment, meta-analysis replicated the classic J-shaped curve, with low-volume drinkers (1.3-24.9 g ethanol/day) having reduced mortality risk (RR = 0.86, 95% CI 0.83-0.90). After adjustment for abstainer biases and quality-related study characteristics, no significant reduction in mortality risk was observed for low-volume drinkers (RR = 0.97, 95% CI 0.88-1.07). Meta-analyses adjusting for these factors find that low-volume alcohol consumption has no net mortality benefit compared with lifetime abstention or occasional drinking.

10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31772-0.results_passage: The prospective China Kadoorie Biobank enrolled 512,715 adults; 161,498 were genotyped for two variants (ALDH2-rs671, ADH1B-rs1229984) that alter alcohol metabolism. Among men, conventional epidemiology showed self-reported alcohol intake had U-shaped associations with ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, and myocardial infarction, with drinkers of about 100 g/week having lower risk than non-drinkers or heavier drinkers. In contrast, genotype-predicted mean alcohol intake had a continuously positive log-linear association with stroke risk (relative risk per 280 g/week 1.58 for intracerebral haemorrhage, 1.27 for ischaemic stroke) and no U-shaped pattern. Genetic epidemiology shows that the apparently protective effects of moderate alcohol intake against stroke are largely non-causal; alcohol consumption uniformly increases blood pressure and stroke risk.

10.1038/bjc.2014.579.results_passage: 572 studies including 486,538 cancer cases were identified across 23 cancer types. Relative risks (RRs) for heavy drinkers compared with nondrinkers/occasional drinkers were 5.13 for oral and pharyngeal cancer, 4.95 for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, 1.44 for colorectal, 2.65 for laryngeal, and 1.61 for breast cancer, with a clear dose-risk relationship for these neoplasms. Heavy drinkers also had significantly higher risk of cancer of the stomach (RR 1.21), liver (2.07), gallbladder (2.64), pancreas (1.19), and lung (1.15). Alcohol increases risk of cancer of the oral cavity and pharynx, oesophagus, colorectum, liver, larynx, and female breast.

figures.label: Figure 3a
figures.caption: Relative risk functions and corresponding 95% confidence intervals describing the dose-response relationship between alcohol consumption and cancer risk obtained by fitting meta-regression models, by cancer site. Abbreviations: AC=adenocarcinoma; RR=relative risk; SCC=squamous cell carcinoma.
figures.shows: Dose-response curves of relative cancer risk versus grams of alcohol consumed per day, plotted separately for multiple cancer sites.

10.1016/S0140-6736(16)30175-1.results_passage: Of 10,625,411 participants in 239 prospective studies, 3,951,455 never-smokers without chronic disease at recruitment (385,879 deaths) were analyzed. All-cause mortality was minimal at 20.0-25.0 kg/m2 and increased significantly both below this range (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.43-1.59 for BMI 15.0-<18.5) and throughout the overweight range (HR 1.20, 95% CI 1.18-1.22 for BMI 27.5-<30.0). The HR for obesity grade 3 (BMI 40.0-<60.0 kg/m2) was 2.76 (95% CI 2.60-2.92). For BMI over 25.0 kg/m2, mortality increased approximately log-linearly with BMI. The associations of both overweight and obesity with higher all-cause mortality were broadly consistent across four continents.

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Association of body-mass index with all-cause mortality, by geographical region. Boxes are plotted against the mean BMI in each group. The HR per 5 kg/m2 higher body-mass index (BMI) and its 95% CI are calculated only for BMI more than 25.0 kg/m2. Analyses restricted to never-smokers without pre-existing chronic disease, excluding the first 5 years of follow-up. The reference category is shown with the arrow.
figures.shows: Dose-response curve of hazard ratio for all-cause mortality across BMI categories, split by geographical region, showing the minimal-risk range around 20-25 kg/m2 and rising risk on both sides.

10.1111/j.1463-1318.2009.01766.x.license: Not in PMC (Wiley, not open access)
10.1111/j.1463-1318.2009.01766.x.results_passage: 29 datasets from 28 articles, including 67,361 incident cases, were analysed. Higher BMI was associated with colon (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.20-1.28) and rectal (1.09, 1.05-1.14) cancers in men, and with colon cancer (1.09, 1.04-1.12) in women, for a 5 kg/m2 increase in BMI. Associations were stronger in men than in women for colon (P < 0.001) and rectal (P = 0.005) cancers, and were generally consistent across geographic populations. Increasing BMI is associated with a modest increased risk of developing colon and rectal cancers, which may translate to large attributable proportions in high-prevalence obese populations.

10.1007/s10654-018-0380-1.results_passage: Thirty-four studies (1,331,468 unique participants) covering 8 exposure-outcome combinations were included. For total sedentary behaviour, the physical-activity-adjusted relationship was non-linear for all-cause mortality (RR per 1 h/day: 1.01 [1.00-1.01] <=8 h/day; 1.04 [1.03-1.05] >8 h/day) and for cardiovascular mortality (1.01 [0.99-1.02] <=6 h/day; 1.04 [1.03-1.04] >6 h/day). Stronger associations were found for TV viewing time: non-linear for all-cause mortality (1.03 [1.01-1.04] <=3.5 h/day; 1.06 [1.05-1.08] >3.5 h/day). A threshold of 6-8 h/day of total sitting and 3-4 h/day of TV viewing was identified, above which risk of major chronic disease outcomes increases.

10.1136/bmj.g4490.results_passage: Sixteen prospective cohort studies (833,234 participants, 56,423 deaths) were eligible. Higher consumption of fruit and vegetables was significantly associated with lower risk of all-cause mortality: pooled hazard ratios were 0.95 (95% CI 0.92 to 0.98) per serving/day of fruit and vegetables combined, 0.94 (0.90 to 0.98) for fruit, and 0.95 (0.92 to 0.99) for vegetables. There was a threshold around five servings of fruit and vegetables a day, after which risk of all-cause mortality did not reduce further. A significant inverse association was also observed for cardiovascular mortality, while fruit and vegetable consumption was not appreciably associated with cancer mortality risk.

figures.label: Fig 3
figures.caption: Dose-response relation between fruit and vegetable consumption and risk of all cause mortality.
figures.shows: Dose-response curve of relative risk of all-cause mortality across increasing servings/day of combined fruit and vegetable consumption, flattening out around five servings/day.

10.3945/ajcn.117.153148.license: Not in PMC (American Society for Nutrition, not open access)
10.3945/ajcn.117.153148.results_passage: A systematic search identified prospective studies on intake of 12 major food groups and risk of all-cause mortality. With increasing intake (per daily serving) of whole grains (RR 0.92), vegetables (RR 0.96), fruits (RR 0.94), nuts (RR 0.76), and fish (RR 0.93), risk of all-cause mortality decreased; higher intake of red meat (RR 1.10) and processed meat (RR 1.23) was associated with increased risk in a linear dose-response meta-analysis. Optimal consumption of risk-decreasing foods results in a 56% reduction of all-cause mortality, whereas consumption of risk-increasing foods is associated with a 2-fold increased risk.

10.1016/j.foodchem.2021.129697.license: Not in PMC (Elsevier, not open access)
10.1016/j.foodchem.2021.129697.results_passage: 72 meta-analyses with 20 unique outcomes for red meat and 19 unique outcomes for processed meat were identified. Red meat consumption was associated with increased risk of overall cancer mortality, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and bladder, breast, colorectal, endometrial, esophageal, gastric, lung, and nasopharyngeal cancer. Processed meat consumption might increase risk of overall cancer mortality and several of the same cancer sites. Dose-response analyses revealed that a 100 g/d increment of red meat and 50 g/d increment of processed meat consumption were associated with 11%-51% and 8%-72% higher risk of multiple cancer outcomes, respectively, with no correlated benefit.

10.1016/j.advnut.2024.100214.results_passage: A dataset of 29 cohorts (23,522,676 person-years) for processed meat and 23 cohorts (17,259,839 person-years) for red meat was compiled from the Global Burden of Disease project's systematic reviews. No significant association was found with 50 g/d red meat consumption using an empirical fit with lower consumption data (RR 0.93, 0.8-1.02) or all consumption levels (1.04, 0.99-1.10), while classical dose-response meta-analysis models showed RRs as high as 1.09 (1.00-1.18) at 50 g/day. Classical model assumptions and inclusion of higher consumption levels influence the association between colorectal cancer and low meat consumption; a no-risk limit of 0 g/d is inconsistent with the evidence.

10.1161/JAHA.117.005947.results_passage: Prospective cohort studies were systematically searched, yielding U-shaped associations between sleep duration and risk of all outcomes, with lowest risk at approximately 7 hours of sleep per day. For all-cause mortality, when sleep duration was <7 hours/day, the pooled relative risk (RR) was 1.06 (95% CI 1.04-1.07) per 1-hour reduction; when >7 hours/day, the pooled RR was 1.13 (95% CI 1.11-1.15) per 1-hour increment. Similar U-shaped patterns were found for total cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease, and stroke. Both short and long sleep duration are associated with increased risk of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Nonlinear dose-response analyses of sleep duration and risk of all-cause mortality (A), total CVD (B), CHD (C), and stroke (D). CHD indicates coronary heart disease; CVD, cardiovascular disease.
figures.shows: U-shaped dose-response curve of relative risk against hours of sleep per day, showing minimum risk around 7 hours and rising risk at both shorter and longer durations.

10.1177/1745691614568352.license: Not in PMC (SAGE, not open access)
10.1177/1745691614568352.results_passage: A literature search of studies from January 1980 to February 2014 found weighted average effect sizes across studies where confounds were statistically controlled: social isolation odds ratio (OR) = 1.29, loneliness OR = 1.26, and living alone OR = 1.32, corresponding to 29%, 26%, and 32% increased likelihood of mortality respectively. No differences were found between measures of objective and subjective social isolation. Results were consistent across gender, length of follow-up, and world region, but initial health status had an influence. The influence of both objective and subjective social isolation on mortality risk is comparable with well-established risk factors for mortality.

10.1016/j.cpcardiol.2023.101670.license: Not in PMC (Elsevier, not open access)
10.1016/j.cpcardiol.2023.101670.results_passage: 18 prospective studies with 7,300,591 individuals followed for a median of 9 years were included. Compared to low long-term exposure to PM2.5 levels, increased exposure resulted in increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.08, 95% CI 1.05-1.11), increased cardiovascular disease (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.00-1.18), and increased cardiovascular disease mortality (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.07-1.18). Increased exposure to PM2.5 is significantly associated with increased risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, and cardiovascular disease mortality. Current federal standards are not low enough to prevent these cardiovascular health effects.

10.1289/ehp.1408882.license: Public domain (Environmental Health Perspectives; without copyright, freely reprintable)
10.1289/ehp.1408882.results_passage: 20 studies met inclusion criteria for a random-effects meta-analysis of nitrogen dioxide (NO2)/NOx exposure and lung cancer. The meta-estimate for change in lung cancer associated with a 10 microg/m3 increase in exposure to NO2 was 4% (95% CI: 1%, 8%); for NOx it was 3% (95% CI: 1%, 5%). The NO2 meta-estimate was robust to different confounding adjustment sets and exposure assessment techniques. Forest plots for measures of traffic volume and distance to roadways largely suggest a modest increase in lung cancer risk. There is consistent evidence of a relationship between NO2, as a proxy for traffic-sourced air pollution exposure, and lung cancer.

10.1136/bmj.a1344.license: CC BY (unrestricted use, distribution, reproduction with citation)
10.1136/bmj.a1344.results_passage: 12 studies with a total of 1,574,299 subjects followed for three to 18 years were included. Cumulative analysis among eight cohorts (514,816 subjects, 33,576 deaths) evaluating overall mortality found that a two-point increase in Mediterranean-diet adherence score was significantly associated with reduced risk of mortality (pooled relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.89 to 0.94). Analyses also showed benefit for cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.91, 0.87 to 0.95), incidence of or mortality from cancer (0.94, 0.92 to 0.96), and incidence of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease (0.87, 0.80 to 0.96). Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with significant improvement in health status.

goals.name: Male vitality / testosterone
goals.definition: Composite goal spanning serum testosterone, vascular/erectile function, lean mass and strength, and subjective libido in adult men.

goals.name: Inflammation / skin
goals.definition: Systemic low-grade inflammation (hs-CRP, IL-6) and skin outcomes (acne severity, sebum production), with insulin/IGF-1 as the mechanistic link between diet and acne.

goals.name: Sleep quality
goals.definition: Composite of circadian alignment (melatonin phase / DLMO), sleep continuity (onset latency), sleep architecture (slow-wave and REM proportion), and subjective sleep quality (PSQI/ISI).

goals.name: Cardiometabolic health
goals.definition: Blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, HbA1c/fasting glucose, insulin sensitivity (HOMA-IR), cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max), and resting heart rate / arterial stiffness (pulse wave velocity) as measurable markers of cardiovascular and metabolic disease risk.

goals.name: Body composition and strength
goals.definition: Fat mass / body fat percentage, fat-free (lean) mass, maximal strength (1RM), waist circumference / visceral adipose tissue, and resting metabolic rate, as driven by resistance training, diet composition and structure, sleep, alcohol, and pharmacology (GLP-1 receptor agonists).

goals.name: Cognition and focus
goals.definition: Working memory, sustained attention/reaction time, episodic memory, global cognition (MMSE/MoCA) in older adults, and processing speed, each tied to a named instrument or task rather than a composite or mortality-style outcome.

goals.name: Mood and anxiety
goals.definition: Depressive symptom severity (PHQ-9, BDI, HAM-D), anxiety symptom severity (GAD-7, STAI, HAM-A, BAI), perceived stress (PSS), and cortisol (salivary, diurnal slope) as the mechanistic stress-axis link. Named-instrument evidence only; mortality and quality-of-life-years outcomes are out of scope.

goals.name: Longevity and mortality risk
goals.definition: Risk of death from any cause (all-cause mortality), death from cardiovascular disease (cardiovascular mortality), and cancer occurrence or death (cancer incidence/mortality), each reported as hazard ratios or relative risks from the literature. This goal is one of eight in the explorer and is not a common unit that other goals' outcomes are converted into; no other goal's endpoints are re-expressed in mortality terms here, and no life-expectancy-years figures are computed from hazard ratios.

paper.design: narrative summary of the author's own meta-analyses of RCTs (72 trials, endurance arm)

edges.verbatim: The meta-analysis on endurance training involved 72 trials and 105 study groups. After weighting for the number of trained participants, training induced significant net reductions of resting and day time ambulatory blood pressure of 3.0/2.4 mmHg (P < 0.001) and 3.3/3.5 mmHg (P < 0.01), respectively. The reduction of resting blood pressure was more pronounced in the 30 hypertensive study groups (-6.9/-4.9) than in the others (-1.9/-1.6; P < 0.001 for all).
edges.key_results: Systemic vascular resistance decreased by 7.1% (P<0.05), plasma noradrenaline by 29% (P<0.001), and plasma renin activity by 20% (P<0.05), pointing to a sympathetic/renin-angiotensin mechanism. Bodyweight fell 1.2 kg, waist circumference 2.8 cm, and body fat 1.4% (all P<0.001), so the BP effect is not isolated from body-composition change. HDL-cholesterol rose 0.032 mmol/L (P<0.05) and the HOMA insulin-resistance index fell by 0.31 units (P<0.01) in the same pooled trials, indicating the training effect is not confined to blood pressure alone.
edges.caveats: This is a 2006 narrative review citing the author's own earlier meta-analyses (Fagard/Cornelissen 2005) rather than presenting new pooled data with a stated total n; original meta-analysis papers were not independently re-extracted.

The authors conclude a diet rich in fruits, vegetables and low-fat dairy with reduced saturated and total fat can substantially lower blood pressure.
edges.caveats: See conflicting 2026 meta-analysis (DOI 10.1016/j.cpcardiol.2026.103397) below: when DASH is compared against OTHER structured diets (Mediterranean, low-carb, etc.) rather than a typical American control diet, the BP advantage disappears (MD=1.30 mmHg, 95% CI -1.54 to 4.14, not significant). The comparator matters: DASH beats a typical Western diet on BP but is not shown to beat other healthy dietary patterns.

edges.verbatim: In two studies involving 3221 participants there was no difference between the omega-3 and placebo group in mini-mental state examination score at final follow-up (following 24 or 40 months of intervention); MD -0.07 (95% CI -0.25 to 0.10). In two studies involving 1043 participants, other tests of cognitive function such as word learning, digit span and verbal fluency showed no beneficial effect of omega-3 PUFA supplementation.
edges.key_results: Cochrane review of randomized trials giving omega-3 PUFA (via gel capsules or fortified margarine) for at least six months to cognitively healthy adults aged 60+. Across 3,221 participants in two trials, there was no difference in MMSE score between omega-3 and placebo groups after 24-40 months. A further two trials (1,043 participants) found no benefit on word learning, digit span, or verbal fluency. No trial examined incident dementia directly. Authors conclude there is no benefit of omega-3 PUFA supplementation on cognitive function in cognitively healthy older people, though longer studies might detect effects the included trials could not.
edges.caveats: This 2012 review is restricted to cognitively healthy older adults; it does not address omega-3 in deficient individuals or in populations with existing cognitive impairment, and a 2025 dose-response meta-analysis pooling broader (including impaired) populations has reported positive associations, which is why this edge is scoped tightly to the matched healthy-older-adult, MMSE-specific claim.

paper.title: Effect of Intensive vs Standard Blood Pressure Control on Probable Dementia: A Randomized Clinical Trial

edges.verbatim: During a total median follow-up of 5.11 years, adjudicated probable dementia occurred in 149 participants in the intensive treatment group vs 176 in the standard treatment group (7.2 vs 8.6 cases per 1000 person-years; hazard ratio [HR], 0.83; 95% CI, 0.67-1.04). Intensive BP control significantly reduced the risk of mild cognitive impairment (14.6 vs 18.3 cases per 1000 person-years; HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.69-0.95) and the combined rate of mild cognitive impairment or probable dementia (20.2 vs 24.1 cases per 1000 person-years; HR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.74-0.97).
edges.key_results: SPRINT MIND randomized 9,361 hypertensive adults aged 50+ to an intensive (<120 mmHg) or standard (<140 mmHg) systolic blood pressure target. Over a median 5.11-year follow-up, intensive treatment significantly reduced the risk of mild cognitive impairment (HR 0.81) and the combined MCI-or-dementia outcome (HR 0.85), but the reduction in the trial's pre-specified primary outcome, probable dementia, did not reach statistical significance (HR 0.83, CI crossing 1). The trial was stopped early (August 2015) for cardiovascular benefit and all-cause mortality, which the authors state likely left too few dementia cases to detect a true effect on that specific, harder-to-diagnose endpoint.
edges.caveats: The primary, hardest endpoint (adjudicated probable dementia) was null; only the secondary MCI endpoint reached significance; outcome is a clinical diagnosis/adjudication rather than a continuous MMSE/MoCA test score, so this edge operationalizes 'global cognition' via validated case-ascertainment rather than a raw test score, unlike the multivitamin, ginkgo, and omega-3 edges above.

paper.title: Single-Dose Creatine Reduces Sleep Deprivation-Induced Deterioration in Cognitive Performance

edges.verbatim: The results show a mitigating effect of creatine on sleep deprivation-induced deterioration in logical and numerical tasks, language-related processing speed, and the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT). Compared to males, females benefit more in logic, PVT and processing speed in language and logic tasks. Our results show that a dose of 0.2 g/kg creatine is associated with a reduced deterioration in cognitive performance during sleep deprivation. Although the effect is less pronounced than with a high dose of 0.35 g/kg, there is still an improvement of up to 12%.
edges.key_results: In the same 21-hour total sleep deprivation RCT described under the sustained-attention edge, a single 0.2 g/kg dose of creatine monohydrate mitigated sleep-deprivation-induced deterioration in language-related processing speed as well as logical/numerical task performance and PVT. Sex-stratified analysis showed a larger benefit in females than males for processing-speed-related tasks. The overall improvement was up to 12% relative to placebo, smaller than the effect seen with a higher 0.35 g/kg dose in the authors' earlier study.
edges.caveats: Small sample (n=29); single acute dose in an acutely sleep-deprived state, not evidence for chronic loading or well-rested individuals; illustrates the conditional_on pattern explicitly requested for creatine (effect concentrated under sleep deprivation) alongside the smaller, low-certainty general-population effect above.

edges.verbatim: Based on data from 40 experimental studies, a small effect of aerobic exercise on time-dependent measures (g = .35) and accuracy (g = .22) in executive function tasks was confirmed. The results further suggest that preadolescent children (g = .54) and older adults (g = .67) compared to other age groups benefit more from aerobic exercise when reaction time is considered as dependent variable.
edges.key_results: Meta-analysis of 40 experimental studies testing a single (acute) bout of moderate aerobic exercise on executive-function task performance. A small overall effect was found on both time-dependent (RT-based, g=.35) and accuracy (g=.22) measures. Age strongly moderated the RT-based effect: preadolescent children and older adults showed substantially larger benefits (g=.54 and g=.67) than other age groups, while aerobic fitness level did not moderate the effect size. Authors suggest older adults and children in particular could use a single exercise bout strategically before tasks demanding high executive control.
edges.caveats: Overall effect (g=.35) is small; the more clinically interesting numbers (g=.54, g=.67) are specific to children and older adults, not the general adult population; 'time-dependent measures' in executive-function tasks is the paper's own operationalization of processing speed, not a single named standardized test.

edges.verbatim: Compared with active controls (eg, usual care, placebo tablet), moderate reductions in depression were found for walking or jogging (n=1210, κ=51, Hedges' g -0.62, 95% credible interval -0.80 to -0.45), yoga (n=1047, κ=33, g -0.55, -0.73 to -0.36), strength training (n=643, κ=22, g -0.49, -0.69 to -0.29), mixed aerobic exercises (n=1286, κ=51, g -0.43, -0.61 to -0.24), and tai chi or qigong (n=343, κ=12, g -0.42, -0.65 to -0.21).
edges.key_results: 218 unique studies with a total of 495 arms and 14,170 participants were included. Compared with active controls, moderate reductions in depression were found for walking or jogging (g -0.62), yoga (g -0.55), and strength training (g -0.49). The effects of exercise were proportional to the intensity prescribed. Exercise is an effective treatment for depression, with walking or jogging, yoga, and strength training more effective than other exercises, particularly when intense. These forms of exercise could be considered alongside psychotherapy and antidepressants as core treatments for depression.
edges.caveats: Confidence in the evidence (CINeMA) was low for walking/jogging and very low for other modalities because only one of 218 included studies met the Cochrane criteria for low risk of bias; participants and staff were unblinded in essentially all trials, so expectancy effects likely inflate the pooled estimates.

The effect size of higher-quality studies (g=0.53) was significantly lower than for lower-quality studies (g=0.90), and this difference remained significant after adjusting for other study characteristics. There is no doubt that CBT is an effective treatment for adult depression, although the effects may have been overestimated until now.

edges.verbatim: Each 1000 IU/day vitamin D3 supplementation slightly reduced depressive symptoms in individuals with and without depression (SMD: -0.32, 95% CI -0.43 to -0.22; GEADE = moderate). edges.key_results: This analysis included 31 trials with 24,189 participants. Each 1000 IU/day vitamin D3 supplementation slightly reduced depressive symptoms overall (SMD -0.32), more pronounced in those with depressive symptoms (SMD -0.57). Trials with follow-up of 24 weeks or less showed much stronger effects than longer trials, with the effect becoming non-significant by 24-52 weeks and reversing direction (non-significantly) beyond 52 weeks. This study suggests that vitamin D3 supplementation may effectively reduce depressive symptoms in the short term, but further high-quality trials are warranted for a conclusive long-term assessment.

edges.evidence_label: Prospective cohort study

edges.effect: Increased long-term PM2.5 exposure associated with increased all-cause mortality, HR 1.08 (95% CI 1.05-1.11)
edges.normalization_method: hazard ratio, high vs low long-term PM2.5 exposure category as defined per included study
edges.population: 7,300,591 individuals pooled across 18 prospective studies, median follow-up 9 years
edges.conditional_on: Exposure cannot be randomized, and effect estimates are sensitive to exposure-assessment method (satellite-derived vs monitor-based) and population age, per companion harmonization studies of this literature; a monotonically increasing risk has also been reported down to the lowest observed PM2.5 levels, i.e. no safe threshold has been identified.

paper.title: PM2.5 and Cardiovascular Health Risks

edges.verbatim: Compared to low long-term exposure to PM 2.5 levels, an increase in exposure to PM 2.5 levels resulted in an increase in all-cause mortality (HR 1.08 95% CI of 1.05-1.11, P < 0.05).
edges.caveats: PM2.5 exposure correlates with lower neighborhood socioeconomic status, proximity to traffic and industry, and other environmental exposures that independently affect health; cohort-level adjustment for individual socioeconomic status is imperfect for an exposure assigned at the neighborhood/residential level.
edges.key_results: We sought to determine the relationship between PM2.5 and cardiovascular disease, cardiovascular events, and all-cause mortality by performing a systematic review and meta-analysis. Compared to low long-term exposure to PM2.5 levels, an increase in exposure resulted in an increase in all-cause mortality (HR 1.08, 95% CI 1.05-1.11). Increased exposure to PM2.5 levels is significantly associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, and cardiovascular disease mortality.

edges.effect: Increased long-term PM2.5 exposure associated with increased cardiovascular disease mortality, HR 1.12 (95% CI 1.07-1.18)
edges.normalization_method: hazard ratio, high vs low long-term PM2.5 exposure category as defined per included study
edges.population: 7,300,591 individuals pooled across 18 prospective studies, median follow-up 9 years
edges.conditional_on: Reported alongside a slightly smaller effect on cardiovascular disease incidence overall (HR 1.09) in the same pooled analysis, i.e. the mortality-specific estimate is at least as large as the incidence estimate.

paper.title: PM2.5 and Cardiovascular Health Risks

edges.verbatim: Similarly, when compared to a low long-term exposure to PM 2.5 levels, an increase in exposure to PM 2.5 levels resulted in an increase in cardiovascular disease (HR 1.09, 95% CI of 1.00-1.18, P < 0.05) and an increase in cardiovascular disease mortality (HR 1.12, 95% CI of 1.07-1.18, P < 0.05).
edges.caveats: Same residential-exposure-assignment and socioeconomic confounding caveats as the all-cause mortality edge for this behavior apply here.
edges.key_results: An increase in exposure to PM2.5 levels resulted in an increase in cardiovascular disease (HR 1.09) and an increase in cardiovascular disease mortality (HR 1.12). Although federal primary and secondary standards are in place, those standards are not low enough to prevent cardiovascular disease health effects. A clinical action guideline is needed specifically for air pollution effects on cardiovascular disease.

edges.evidence_label: Prospective cohort study

edges.effect: Each 10 ug/m3 increase in NO2 (a traffic-related air pollution proxy) associated with a 4% increase in lung cancer risk (95% CI 1%-8%)
edges.normalization_method: relative risk per 10 ug/m3 increase in NO2 exposure
edges.population: 20 studies meeting inclusion criteria for the NO2/lung cancer meta-estimate
edges.conditional_on: This edge uses nitrogen dioxide (NO2) as a proxy for traffic-sourced air pollution, not PM2.5 mass concentration directly; a dedicated PM2.5-specific pooled dose-response estimate for lung cancer with a cleanly quotable number could not be retrieved within the research budget for this file (see cut_candidates), so this NO2/traffic-proxy meta-analysis is used instead and the exposure metric should not be treated as interchangeable with the PM2.5 estimates in the other two edges for this behavior.

paper.title: Lung Cancer and Exposure to Nitrogen Dioxide and Traffic: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
paper.design: meta-analysis of prospective cohort and case-control studies

edges.verbatim: The meta-estimate for the change in lung cancer associated with a 10-μg/m3 increase in exposure to NO2 was 4% (95% CI: 1%, 8%).
edges.caveats: NO2 and PM2.5 are correlated but distinct pollutants from overlapping but not identical sources (NO2 is more specifically traffic-associated); this is why this edge is treated as a proxy rather than direct PM2.5-cancer evidence. Trim-and-fill analysis in the source paper suggests that if publication bias exists, the true effect may be even larger than reported, not smaller.
edges.key_results: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of research examining the relationship of nitrogen oxides and traffic-related air pollution exposure with lung cancer. The meta-estimate for the change in lung cancer associated with a 10-ug/m3 increase in exposure to NO2 was 4% (95% CI: 1%, 8%). We found consistent evidence of a relationship between NO2, as a proxy for traffic-sourced air pollution exposure, with lung cancer. The International Agency for Research on Cancer recently classified outdoor air pollution and particulate matter as carcinogenic (Group 1).

edges.evidence_label: Prospective cohort study

edges.effect: A 2-point increase in Mediterranean diet adherence score associated with a 9% reduction in overall mortality (pooled RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.89-0.94)
edges.normalization_method: pooled relative risk per 2-point increase in a priori adherence score
edges.population: 514,816 subjects across 8 cohorts (overall mortality analysis), part of a total of 1,574,299 subjects across 12 cohorts in the full review, followed 3-18 years
edges.conditional_on: Adherence measured via a composite a priori diet score (higher = closer to the traditional Mediterranean pattern of high fruit/vegetable/legume/whole-grain/olive-oil intake, moderate fish, low red meat); this is an adherence gradient rather than a specific quantified nutrient dose.

paper.title: Adherence to Mediterranean diet and health status: meta-analysis

edges.verbatim: The cumulative analysis among eight cohorts (514,816 subjects and 33,576 deaths) evaluating overall mortality in relation to adherence to a Mediterranean diet showed that a two point increase in the adherence score was significantly associated with a reduced risk of mortality (pooled relative risk 0.91, 95% confidence interval 0.89 to 0.94).
edges.caveats: Adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet correlates with higher socioeconomic status, more physical activity, and less smoking in the populations studied (mostly Mediterranean and other European cohorts), and observational dietary-pattern cohorts cannot fully separate the diet's own effect from this broader healthy-lifestyle clustering.
edges.key_results: The cumulative analysis among eight cohorts evaluating overall mortality in relation to adherence to a Mediterranean diet showed that a two-point increase in the adherence score was significantly associated with a reduced risk of mortality (pooled relative risk 0.91). Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with a significant improvement in health status, as seen by a significant reduction in overall mortality (9%). These results seem to be clinically relevant for public health, in particular for encouraging a Mediterranean-like dietary pattern for primary prevention of major chronic diseases.

edges.effect: A 2-point increase in Mediterranean diet adherence score associated with a 9% reduction in cardiovascular mortality (pooled RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.87-0.95)

paper.title: Adherence to Mediterranean diet and health status: meta-analysis

edges.verbatim: Likewise, the analyses showed a beneficial role for greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet on cardiovascular mortality (pooled relative risk 0.91, 0.87 to 0.95), incidence of or mortality from cancer (0.94, 0.92 to 0.96), and incidence of Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease (0.87, 0.80 to 0.96).
edges.caveats: Same healthy-lifestyle clustering caveat as the all-cause mortality edge for this behavior applies; the 2008 publication date makes this an older synthesis relative to more recent Mediterranean-diet RCT evidence (e.g. PREDIMED) that addresses cardiovascular events but not primarily long-term mortality with comparable pooled precision.
edges.key_results: The analyses showed a beneficial role for greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet on cardiovascular mortality (pooled relative risk 0.91). Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with a significant reduction in mortality from cardiovascular diseases (9%). These results seem to be clinically relevant for public health, in particular for encouraging a Mediterranean-like dietary pattern for primary prevention of major chronic diseases.
